disease_info: Bipolar I Disorder with Psychotic Features is characterized by at least one full manic episode, often with marked functional impairment, that may be accompanied by delusions or hallucinations congruent or incongruent with mood. Episodes typically develop over days to weeks and can last weeks to months, with intervening periods of partial or full remission; depressive episodes are common but not required for diagnosis. Psychotic features usually emerge at the more severe end of mania or depression and help distinguish Bipolar I from Bipolar II and cyclothymia, as well as from primary psychotic disorders like schizophrenia where mood symptoms are not as prominent or temporally linked. The course is often recurrent, influenced by stress, sleep disruption, and biological vulnerability, and may be complicated by impaired insight, risky behavior, and strained social and occupational functioning.

narrative.stressor: In the months leading up to her episode, Eunhae had been picking up extra shifts at the long‑term care facility due to staffing shortages while also coordinating medical appointments and translation for her aging parents, one of whom had a recent minor stroke. Her previously structured routine of early‑morning tai chi, careful budgeting, and quiet evenings gradually gave way to fragmented sleep and a sense of responsibility that she had to personally safeguard every detail of her patients’ and parents’ care. Over roughly two months she became increasingly overextended at work and at home, insisting on taking on more tasks and clashing with colleagues and family when they questioned her decisions, which led to noticeable strain in her marriage and complaints from coworkers about her behavior. The situation became clinically significant when she began insisting she alone could prevent serious harm to her patients and parents, refused to leave work or sleep, and her husband and charge nurse brought her to the emergency department after she confronted a physician and tried to override medical orders.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t slow down—I have too many important things to take care of and I feel driven to keep doing more, day and night.”

narrative.stressor: Aaron’s episode emerged in the context of several losses in quick succession: a close friend from his walking club died suddenly, and his younger brother was diagnosed with advanced cancer, prompting frequent visits and late‑night drives back to his hometown. He threw himself into memorial projects and community arts events honoring local heritage, spending long stretches alone in his workshop and increasingly neglecting sleep and basic routines while insisting that his artwork carried a special significance for preserving the town’s spirit. Over the next two months, his wife and book‑club friends noticed his conversations becoming more intense and tangential, along with growing tension at home as he dismissed their concerns and redirected household money and time toward his projects. When he began asserting that his paintings contained messages meant specifically for national leaders and mailed several unsolicited portfolios to government offices, his worried wife persuaded him to see a psychiatrist at the local clinic.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I know my paintings have an important message for the people running this country, and no one seems to understand that.”

narrative.stressor: For Sara, the onset coincided with a period of rapid growth at her startup, where she was promoted and tasked with overseeing multiple new product launches while informally mentoring junior staff and studying for the GMAT in her spare time. What began as long hours and high energy at work escalated over a few weeks into an unsustainable pace: back‑to‑back meetings, late‑night strategy sessions at coffee shops, and weekend travel for networking events, with her normal exercise and social routines becoming increasingly erratic. Over the following two months, colleagues noticed her becoming increasingly forceful and difficult to interrupt in meetings, dominating discussions and sending streams of late‑night messages about sweeping process overhauls that were only loosely connected to the team’s plans. The situation reached a crisis when a senior executive confronted her about her behavior after she spoke nonstop through a presentation and derailed a major client call, and HR strongly recommended she seek an urgent psychiatric evaluation before returning to full responsibilities.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Once I start talking, I just can’t seem to stop—I feel like I have to get every idea out all at once and people keep telling me I’m overwhelming them.”
